17.text: Hut. — The small village that in former times existed in Anadyr Bay,

18.text: had huts constructed of wood and covered with earth and sod.

19.text: Two families of those living in Veᵋñ (Mariinsky Post), not far from the

20.text: site of the village mentioned, still construct for their winter lodges small huts

21.text: with wooden frames covered over with earth and stones. The hut has a hole

22.text: in the roof for the escape of smoke, and within is a sleeping-room of the

23.text: usual shape. The hut has a square wooden door covered with scraps of

24.text: reindeer-skin for greater warmth. Plate XVII, Fig. 2, represents one of these

25.text: huts. The poles in the front serve for hanging dried fish on.

26.text: A few Chukchee families of the Middle Anadyr live in wooden huts

27.text: somewhat similar to the Yakut “yurta.” These were copied from the yurtas

28.text: of the Anadyr Russians, who of late years, however, have replaced their

29.text: yurtas with log-cabins of the usual Northeast-Siberian type. In ancient times

30.text: wooden huts of this type may have been in more common use in this territory.

31.text: Remains of huts found on the Bear Islands are more or less of this type.

32.text: In the deserted villages of the Yukaghir situated on the Middle Omolon,

33.text: and inhabited about seventy-five years ago, I have seen huts of the same

34.text: type. It is not easy to decide whether this type of dwelling is due to Yakut

35.text: influence, or whether it is an ancient type that developed independently. The

36.text: construction of the fireplace differs in all of them from that of the Yakut

37.text: houses. They had no stove with wooden chimney, but simply a central

38.text: hearth, with a square hole in the roof just above it. In modern times the

39.text: Yakut, arrangement of the fireplace has been copied by most of the Russians
